page.text:
While propositional logic provides the rules for combining complete,
self-contained assertions, it is blind to the internal anatomy of
statements. In propositional logic, the statements 'Every continuous
function on a closed interval is bounded' and '$7$ is a prime number' are
merely opaque atomic variables $P$ and $Q$. Propositional logic cannot
express the fact that $7$ possesses a property shared by other numbers,
nor can it account for the word 'every'.

To capture the full depth of mathematical reasoning, we must peer inside
assertions. In 1879, Gottlob Frege revolutionized logic by replacing the
traditional subject-predicate grammar of classical philosophy with the
mathematical concept of a *function*. An assertion is understood as a
property or relation—a *predicate*—applied to one or more mathematical
objects. By introducing *quantifiers* that govern variables ranging over
specified domains, we obtain *first-order predicate logic*, the
expressive medium in which modern mathematics is written.
